instance_type: HPE ProLiant DL380 Gen10, one Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz (main throughput rig); latency-distribution SET block and p50 figures from redis.io benchmark docs
workload_shape: SET with 100,000 random keys (-r 100000), 1,000,000 requests, NO pipelining → single-operation latency. 3-byte payload. p50 figures are from a separate pipelined (-P 16) run and represent a lower anchor.
concurrency_model: 50 parallel clients (redis-benchmark default), single-threaded Redis server; keep-alive on
config_notes: Value 1.0 ms reflects the documented non-pipelined SET distribution where 99.76% of single operations complete within 1 ms (3-byte payload, 50 clients, keep-alive). Median single-op latency is sub-millisecond: the docs' p50 figures (pipelined) are 0.479 ms (SET) / 0.391 ms (GET), used as the lower confidence bound. Band [0.4, 1.5] ms honestly spans documented median-to-near-max and accounts for hardware variance; these are LOOPBACK/local numbers — real-world latency adds network RTT (~200 us for 1 Gbit/s, ~30 us Unix socket per redis.io). Redis docs note most commands process in sub-microsecond range; observed latency is dominated by network + roundtrips. T1 vendor source.

citations.source: Redis official documentation — How fast is Redis? (redis-benchmark)
citations.note: Non-pipelined SET: 1,000,000 requests, 50 parallel clients, 3-byte payload, keep-alive on, 100,000 random keys; 99.76% <= 1 ms, 99.98% <= 2 ms, 100% <= 3 ms; 72,144.87 rps. Pipelined (-P 16) on MacBook Air 11": SET p50=0.479 ms, GET p50=0.391 ms. Main throughput rig: HPE ProLiant DL380 Gen10, Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz, 256-byte payload, 50 clients, 5M requests, loopback. All loopback/local — excludes external network RTT.

instance_type: AWS RDS db.m8gd.4xlarge (16 vCPU / 64 GB, NVMe-backed)
workload_shape: pgbench default TPC-B-like (read-write OLTP mix: per-transaction it updates pgbench_accounts/branches/tellers + inserts into pgbench_history), scale factor 6849 (~100 GB dataset), 10-minute run (-T 600)
concurrency_model: 256 concurrent pgbench clients, 16 threads (-c 256 -j 16), prepared statements (-M prepared)
config_notes: VALUE IS RPS (TPS), not cost. pgbench reports transactions/second; here 1 transaction = 1 TPC-B-like write transaction (3 UPDATE + 1 SELECT + 1 INSERT). The number is highly sensitive to: instance vCPU count (4 vCPU ~6.2k vs 16 vCPU ~8-29k), storage (local NVMe vs network EBS), client concurrency vs vCPU ratio (over-subscription collapses TPS — see the 783 TPS contended RDS case), dataset-in-RAM ratio (scale 6849 ~100GB exceeds the 64GB RAM, so disk I/O matters), and read/write mix (a read-only pgbench -S workload would be far higher). Do NOT apply this figure to a different instance size, storage class, or read-heavy workload without re-deriving. Per-provider managed Postgres tuning varies widely on identical hardware (8133 RDS vs 28668 ClickHouse-managed on the same 16-vCPU class).

citations.source: ClickHouse Blog — PostgresBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Postgres Services
citations.note: AWS RDS db.m8gd.4xlarge (16 vCPU / 64 GB), PostgreSQL 17/18, scale factor 6849 (~100 GB), pgbench TPC-B-like read-write, `pgbench -c 256 -j 16 -T 600 -M prepared -P 30`, 10-min run = 8133 TPS. Same source, same 16-vCPU/64GB class & scale: ClickHouse-managed 28668, Crunchy Bridge 14790, Aurora 12628, Neon 8563; m8gd.xlarge (4 vCPU/16GB) = 6172. AWS region not stated.

citations.source: Severalnines — Benchmarking Managed PostgreSQL Cloud Solutions: Part Two - Amazon RDS
citations.note: Corroborating/order-of-magnitude only. Amazon RDS db.r4.2xlarge (8 vCPU / 61 GiB), PostgreSQL 11.1, scale factor 10000, 1000 clients/1000 threads, 600s, read-write TPC-B: 'tps = 783.610726 (excluding connections establishing)', avg latency 1274.340 ms. This is a deliberately over-contended config (1000 clients on 8 vCPUs) measuring contention, not peak throughput — illustrates how TPS collapses when clients >> vCPUs.

instance_type: 8 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM, Intel Xeon E5-2699 v4 @ 2.2 GHz (Dell PowerEdge bare metal)
workload_shape: Reverse-proxy / load-balancer mode: client -> NGINX Plus -> upstream web server. 1 KB response size. Keepalive on both client and upstream legs (keepalive_timeout 300s, keepalive_requests 1000000). 3-minute (180s) sustained test runs.
concurrency_model: Event-driven NGINX Plus reverse proxy; 1 worker process per CPU core (8 workers). Load generated with wrk: one copy per CPU, 50 TCP connections per copy.
config_notes: Source = official NGINX/F5 "Sizing Guide for Deploying NGINX Plus on Bare Metal Servers" (T1 vendor datasheet, published 2019-11-11), retrieved via Internet Archive OCR full-text. Full per-core RPS scale documented in the same table: 2 cores=90,000 RPS; 4 cores=175,000 RPS; 8 cores=350,000 RPS; 16 cores=650,000 RPS; 32 cores=1,000,000 RPS; 44 cores=1,200,000 RPS. Reported value 350,000 RPS chosen as a representative single mid-range "per-instance" point (8 cores) rather than the 32/44-core ceiling. This is NGINX Plus reverse-proxy/load-balancer mode (not bare web-server mode). Methodology corroborated by F5 "NGINX Plus Sizing Guide: How We Tested" (50 TCP connections per wrk copy, 1 KB file, 3-min runs, 2x Xeon E5-2699, keepalive_timeout 300s, keepalive_requests 1000000). T1 band set at +/-10% (315,000-385,000). Caveat: these are vendor-stated expected-performance figures for sized hardware, slightly idealized; OCR rendered the clock as "22.GHz" which is the published 2.2 GHz. Open-source NGINX on cloud VMs with smaller payloads and TLS will be substantially lower; misapply with care.

citations.source: NGINX/F5 — Sizing Guide for Deploying NGINX Plus on Bare Metal Servers (official datasheet, published 11 Nov 2019; retrieved via Internet Archive OCR full-text)
citations.note: NGINX Plus reverse-proxy/load-balancer mode; 8 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM; Intel Xeon E5-2699 v4 @ 2.2 GHz (Dell PowerEdge bare metal); 1 KB response size; keepalive on client and upstream legs => 350,000 RPS. Table also: 2c=90k, 4c=175k, 16c=650k, 32c=1.0M, 44c=1.2M RPS.
